Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

OXON HILL, Maryland (CNN) -- Crew members of the Maersk Alabama, safely back in the United States after being attacked by pirates last week off Somalia, recounted their ordeal Thursday. Navy personnel recover the lifeboat from which Maersk Alabama Capt. Richard Phillips was rescued Sunday. "They start firing before they climb, with AK-47," crew member Zahid Reza said. "I was scared for my life. I was almost close to that. And they tried to shoot me many times," he said, pointing to his head. "Pointing gun all over. Here, there, in the back." Pirates tried three times to board the U.S.-flagged cargo ship before their fourth attempt was successful, fellow crew member William Rios said, adding that the groups of pirates were different but that he thinks they were working together. Rios said he was working on deck when he was called back to lock down the ship. Then, he said, there were gunshots, and an alarm went off to alert all crew members to wake up and get on deck. "We went to our training," he said, declining to provide details: "If I tell you all what we did, pirates, they would know."  Watch the crew praise their captain » . The pirates intended to ask for a $3 million ransom, Reza said. He said he and the ship's chief engineer took one of the pirates hostage. Reza said he persuaded the pirate -- whom he described as a young man, maybe 18 or 19 -- to trust him, pointing out that he is Bangladeshi and the pirate was Somali. "His name is Abdul," Reza said. "I told him, 'Trust me. I am Muslim; you are Muslim.' " He told Abdul he would take him to the engine room to find more crew members. When they got there, the room was dark, he said, and he didn't know the ship's chief engineer was in there. He said the chief engineer jumped the pirate first, then Reza stabbed him with his knife, and the two men tied the pirate's hands and feet. Reza said he intended to kill the youth, but the chief engineer told him, "No, we need him alive."  Watch Reza talk about wanting to kill the pirate » . "He was fighting me and chief engineer, to get away from us. A lot of yelling, shouting and screaming." Rios said he went to the lifeboat, where Capt. Richard Phillips was being held, to exchange Abdul for Phillips but was unsuccessful. The captain -- who offered himself as a hostage in exchange for the freedom of his crew -- was rescued by U.S. Navy SEALs on Sunday. The SEALs, on the nearby guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, fatally shot three pirates and rescued Phillips. A fourth pirate was arrested. "I feel great they got killed," Reza said. "I am happy." He said he was proud of the Navy. Phillips arrived in Mombasa, Kenya, aboard the Bainbridge on Thursday. The crew arrived at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland overnight.  Watch crew arrive in U.S. » . Rios said Phillips is "outstanding; he's extraordinary; he's [a] very brave man." Another crew member, John White, said they were "damn lucky to be alive." Rios called for more security in the Gulf of Aden. "Put more military to patrol the waterway for us transporting material back and forth," he said. "... All the countries got to get involved with this." Reza echoed the call. "I think government should get involved," he said. "They should think about our safety, yes. ... This piracy is getting bigger and bigger." CNN's Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
**OXON HILL, Maryland (CNN) —** Crew members of the *Maersk Alabama*, safely back in the United States after being attacked by pirates off Somalia last week, recounted their ordeal Thursday.

Navy personnel recovered the lifeboat from which *Maersk Alabama* Capt. Richard Phillips was rescued Sunday.

“They start firing before they climb, with AK-47,” crew member Zahid Reza said. “I was scared for my life. I was almost close to that. And they tried to shoot me many times,” he added, pointing to his head. “Pointing gun all over. Here, there, in the back.”

Pirates made three unsuccessful attempts to board the U.S.-flagged cargo ship before succeeding on their fourth, fellow crew member William Rios said. He added that although the groups of pirates were different, he believed they were working together.

Rios said he was working on deck when he was called back to help lock down the ship. Gunshots followed, he said, and an alarm sounded, alerting all crew members to wake up and report to the deck.

“We went to our training,” he said, declining to provide details. “If I tell you all what we did, pirates, they would know.”

*Watch the crew praise their captain »*

The pirates intended to demand a $3 million ransom, Reza said. He said that he and the ship’s chief engineer took one of the pirates hostage.

Reza said he persuaded the pirate—whom he described as a young man, perhaps 18 or 19—to trust him, pointing out that he is Bangladeshi and the pirate was Somali.

“His name is Abdul,” Reza said. “I told him, ‘Trust me. I am Muslim; you are Muslim.’”

He told Abdul that he would take him to the engine room to find more crew members. When they arrived, the room was dark, Reza said, and he did not know that the ship’s chief engineer was inside.

The chief engineer jumped the pirate first, Reza said. Reza then stabbed the pirate with his knife, and the two men tied the pirate’s hands and feet.

Reza said he intended to kill the young man, but the chief engineer told him, “No, we need him alive.”

*Watch Reza talk about wanting to kill the pirate »*

“He was fighting me and chief engineer, to get away from us. A lot of yelling, shouting and screaming.”

Rios said he went to the lifeboat where Capt. Richard Phillips was being held and attempted to exchange Abdul for Phillips, but the effort was unsuccessful.

Phillips—who offered himself as a hostage in exchange for his crew’s freedom—was rescued Sunday by U.S. Navy SEALs. Operating from the nearby guided-missile destroyer USS *Bainbridge*, the SEALs fatally shot three pirates and rescued Phillips. A fourth pirate was arrested.

“I feel great they got killed,” Reza said. “I am happy.” He added that he was proud of the Navy.

Phillips arrived in Mombasa, Kenya, aboard the *Bainbridge* on Thursday. The crew arrived overnight at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland.

*Watch the crew arrive in the U.S. »*

Rios described Phillips as “outstanding; he’s extraordinary; he’s [a] very brave man.”

Another crew member, John White, said they were “damn lucky to be alive.”

Rios called for greater security in the Gulf of Aden.

“Put more military to patrol the waterway for us transporting material back and forth,” he said. “... All the countries got to get involved with this.”

Reza echoed that appeal.

“I think government should get involved,” he said. “They should think about our safety, yes. ... This piracy is getting bigger and bigger.”

CNN’s Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
**OXON HILL, Maryland (CNN) —** Members of the *Maersk Alabama* crew, who returned safely to the United States after pirates attacked their ship off Somalia the previous week, described the experience Thursday.

Navy personnel retrieved the lifeboat from which *Maersk Alabama* Capt. Richard Phillips was rescued Sunday.

Crewman Zahid Reza said the attackers began shooting AK-47 rifles before climbing aboard. He said he feared he would be killed and that the pirates repeatedly aimed their weapons at his head, back and other parts of his body.

According to fellow crew member William Rios, the pirates made three unsuccessful attempts to board the U.S.-flagged cargo vessel before succeeding on the fourth. Although different groups carried out the attempts, Rios said he believed they were cooperating.

Rios was working on deck when he received orders to return and help secure the vessel. He then heard gunfire, and an alarm sounded, telling crew members to wake up and report to the deck.

The sailors responded according to their training, Rios said, but he declined to explain their tactics because revealing them could help pirates in future attacks.

The crew also praised its captain in a video.

Reza said the hijackers planned to demand a $3 million ransom. He and the ship’s chief engineer managed to capture one of the pirates.

The pirate, whom Reza identified as Abdul, appeared to be about 18 or 19 years old. Reza said he gained the young man’s confidence by noting that Reza was Bangladeshi, Abdul was Somali and both were Muslims.

Reza told Abdul that he would lead him to the engine room, where other crew members could supposedly be found. The room was dark when they entered, and Reza said he did not realize the chief engineer was already there.

The chief engineer attacked the pirate first. Reza then stabbed Abdul with a knife, after which the two crewmen bound the captive’s hands and feet.

Reza said he wanted to kill the young pirate, but the chief engineer stopped him, saying they needed to keep Abdul alive. A video showed Reza discussing his desire to kill the attacker.

According to Reza, Abdul struggled violently to escape, and the confrontation involved extensive yelling, shouting and screaming.

Rios said he approached the lifeboat where Phillips was being held and attempted to trade Abdul for the captain, but the exchange failed.

Phillips had volunteered to become a hostage so his crew could go free. U.S. Navy SEALs rescued him Sunday. Operating from the nearby guided-missile destroyer USS *Bainbridge*, the SEALs shot and killed three pirates, freed Phillips and took a fourth pirate into custody.

Reza said he was pleased that the three pirates had been killed and expressed pride in the Navy.

Phillips reached Mombasa, Kenya, aboard the *Bainbridge* on Thursday. His crew had arrived overnight at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland, an arrival also shown in video footage.

Rios described Phillips as exceptional, extraordinarily courageous and an outstanding captain. Another sailor, John White, said the crew was extremely fortunate to have survived.

Rios urged authorities to increase security in the Gulf of Aden by deploying more military forces to patrol the sea route used to transport goods. He said every country needed to take part.

Reza made a similar appeal, saying governments should become involved and give greater consideration to crew safety because piracy was continuing to expand.

CNN’s Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to the report.

Recounting the ordeal, they said the pirates made four attempts to board the U.S.-flagged cargo ship. During the assault, the attackers fired AK-47 rifles before eventually gaining access to the vessel.

The crew responded by following emergency procedures they had practiced in training. As alarms sounded and gunfire erupted, crew members secured key areas of the ship and carried out lockdown measures intended to prevent the pirates from taking full control. The attackers reportedly planned to demand a ransom of $3 million.

During the confrontation, crew member Zahid Reza and the chief engineer lured a young pirate into the engine room. They managed to overpower and stab him, but kept him alive and held him as a hostage. Their actions became part of the crew’s broader effort to resist the hijacking and protect those aboard.

In April 2009, crew members aboard the U.S.-flagged cargo ship *Maersk Alabama* faced a violent pirate attack while sailing several hundred miles off the coast of Somalia. The crew later recalled that pirates had approached the ship more than once, using small, fast boats and weapons to intimidate the sailors and force their way aboard. When four Somali pirates finally succeeded in boarding, the crew quickly put its security training into practice.

Most crew members moved into secure areas of the vessel, shut down key systems, and used their knowledge of the ship’s layout to avoid capture. They maintained communication with one another and worked to deny the attackers control of the ship. During the confrontation, crew members managed to overpower and detain one of the pirates, creating an opportunity to negotiate with the others.

The crew attempted to exchange the captured attacker for Captain Richard Phillips, who had been taken hostage. Although the pirate was released, Phillips was not returned. Instead, the pirates fled in an enclosed lifeboat with the captain, beginning a tense standoff with U.S. naval forces. Phillips remained a hostage for several days as Navy ships tracked the lifeboat and tried to secure his release.

The crisis ended when U.S. Navy SEAL snipers killed three of the pirates after commanders determined that Phillips’s life was in immediate danger. The remaining pirate, who had earlier boarded a Navy vessel for medical treatment and negotiations, was taken into custody. Phillips was rescued and reunited with his crew.

Accounts from the *Maersk Alabama* sailors emphasized that the outcome depended not only on the military rescue but also on the crew’s discipline and coordinated resistance. By following established procedures, securing the vessel, disabling systems, and acting together, they prevented the pirates from taking full control of the ship and reduced the number of hostages. Their experience became a prominent example of how preparation, communication, and teamwork can help merchant crews respond effectively to piracy at sea.

Oxon Hill is a community in Prince George’s County, Maryland, located just southeast of Washington, D.C., along the Potomac River. Its convenient position near the Capital Beltway makes it an important gateway between Maryland, Virginia, and the nation’s capital.

## Maersk Alabama crew recounts pirate attack and dramatic captain rescue

**NORFOLK, Virginia —** Crew members aboard the *Maersk Alabama* described locking themselves inside the cargo ship’s engine room, disabling key systems and capturing a young Somali pirate during the April 2009 attack that ended with the U.S. Navy’s rescue of Capt. Richard Phillips.

The U.S.-flagged vessel was carrying food aid toward Kenya on April 8 when four armed pirates boarded it in the Indian Ocean, hundreds of miles off Somalia’s coast.

According to crew accounts, Phillips and other officers attempted evasive maneuvers as the pirates approached. Once the attackers were aboard, much of the crew retreated to a secure area, cut power and used their knowledge of the ship to resist the takeover.

The sailors eventually seized one of the pirates, later identified as Abduwali Muse. But the standoff shifted when the other three pirates left the ship in an enclosed lifeboat with Phillips as their hostage. The crew released Muse during an attempted exchange, but Phillips was not freed.

U.S. Navy ships, including the guided-missile destroyer USS *Bainbridge*, soon reached the area and began negotiations. Phillips remained in the cramped lifeboat for several days as tensions mounted and officials grew concerned that his life was in immediate danger.

On April 12, Navy SEAL snipers positioned aboard the *Bainbridge* simultaneously shot and killed the three pirates holding Phillips. U.S. officials said the action was authorized after commanders determined that the pirates were threatening the captain with weapons.

Phillips was recovered unharmed and taken aboard the Navy ship for medical evaluation. Muse, who had boarded the *Bainbridge* for treatment and negotiations, was taken into U.S. custody. He later pleaded guilty to federal charges and received a prison sentence of more than 33 years.

Crew members credited their survival to preparation, teamwork and their familiarity with the vessel. Their resistance prevented the pirates from maintaining control of the *Maersk Alabama*, even as Phillips’ captivity became the focus of an extraordinary U.S. military operation.

The incident drew worldwide attention to piracy off Somalia and renewed debate over security aboard commercial ships traveling through one of the world’s most dangerous maritime corridors.
